issues.legal_issue: An earlier interdepartmental communication that leaves the matter for another authority to finalise does not exhaust the Central Government’s revisional power when it records no decision by that Government.
material_facts: The Chief Settlement Commissioner had upheld the separate allotments.
A later communication from a Joint Secretary said the matter should be finalised on the basis of existing findings and returned the record to the Punjab Government, asking it to finalise the case.
The Punjab Government subsequently sought revision, and the Central Government issued an order setting aside the Chief Settlement Commissioner’s decision.
issues.conclusion: The communication was not a decision by the Central Government in exercise of its revisional power. The later order was the first exercise of that power and was not without jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 33 of the Punjab Refugees (Registration of Land Claims) Act, 1948, the Central Government has broad power to call for proceedings and pass an order in relation to them. Whether a communication is a decision depends on its substance, not its form: D.N. Roy and S.K. Bannerjee v. State of Bihar supports treating a letter as a decision when it actually conveys the Government’s decision. The Court assumed, without deciding, that the power could not be exercised more than once in the same proceeding.

predicates.challenge_to_later_revisional_order: The proceeding challenged a later order made by a higher authority exercising revisional power over an earlier administrative order.
predicates.earlier_communication_left_finalisation_: An earlier communication returned the record to another authority and asked that authority to finalise the matter.
predicates.earlier_communication_recorded_no_govern: The earlier communication expressed views or recommendations but did not record a decision by the government holding the revisional power.
predicates.later_order_exercised_revisional_power: The government holding the revisional power later made an order revising the earlier administrative decision.

issues.definition: When a challenged revisional order follows an earlier communication that left finalisation to another authority and recorded no government decision, the later order is within jurisdiction if it is the first exercise of revisional power.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate on the death of a respondent below when no relief was sought against that respondent and the appeal concerns parties adversely affected by the challenged decision.
material_facts: The deceased person had been a respondent in the High Court, not a petitioner.
No relief had been claimed against him, and he had not been directed to surrender the land.
The petitioners before the High Court were adversely affected by the decision challenged in the appeal.
issues.conclusion: The death of the respondent did not cause the appeal to abate.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that abatement did not follow in these circumstances because the deceased respondent was not the person seeking relief below, no relief was sought against him, and his death did not affect the appeal concerning the petitioners who were adversely affected.

predicates.appeal_from_adverse_decision: The proceeding is an appeal by persons adversely affected by the decision under challenge.
predicates.deceased_person_was_respondent_below: A person who died during the appeal had been a respondent in the proceeding below.
predicates.no_relief_was_sought_against_deceased_pe: The proceeding below sought no relief against the person who died.
predicates.deceased_person_was_not_required_to_surr: The person who died had not been required by the challenged decision to surrender the property at issue.

issues.definition: An appeal by persons adversely affected by a decision does not abate on a respondent’s death when no relief was sought against that respondent and the decision did not require that respondent to surrender property.

issues.legal_issue: A claim to separate allotments based on an alleged oral partition may be rejected when the contemporaneous claims and records do not support the partition and the claim appears to have been raised later to obtain a greater allotment.
material_facts: The father’s initial land claims described the land as his own and did not mention a partition with his sons or wife.
Separate claims based on an alleged oral partition were made later.
There was no written partition document, and the revenue records named the father alone as owner.
There were no records showing separate payment of land revenue by the other claimants, and they had not objected when the father first claimed the land.
issues.conclusion: The Court found the alleged partition to be an unsupported afterthought and held that the other claimants were not entitled to separate allotments on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: In reviewing the challenged administrative decision, the Court treated the absence of documentary support and the inconsistency between the initial claim and later separate claims as relevant considerations undermining the alleged partition. It declined to re-evaluate the evidence in the certiorari proceeding and found no basis to interfere with the administrative findings.

rule.if: certiorari_review_of_allotment_decision and initial_claim_named_one_owner and later_separate_claims_relied_on_oral_partition and no_partition_document_exists and ownership_records_named_one_owner

predicates.certiorari_review_of_allotment_decision: The proceeding sought certiorari review of an administrative decision about allotments.
predicates.initial_claim_named_one_owner: The initial claim identified one person as the owner without mentioning a division of the property among family members.
predicates.later_separate_claims_relied_on_oral_par: Other claimants later sought separate allotments on the basis of an alleged oral division of the property.
predicates.no_partition_document_exists: The claimants produced no written document recording the alleged division.
predicates.ownership_records_named_one_owner: The available ownership records identified one person alone as the owner.

issues.definition: In certiorari review of an allotment decision, separate allotments based on an alleged oral division are unsupported when the initial claim named one owner, later separate claims relied on that division, no written record of it exists, and the ownership records named one owner.
